cards.H-SOM: The body's trauma reactions may persist after objective danger is over, even when the person knows consciously that they are safe. With complex/developmental trauma, directly working on the deepest memory can overwhelm someone; gentle gradual work around the edges may suffice. Attribution: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron uses the phrase 'feather touch' for gentle approach; Peter Levine, founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle edge-work 'pendulation'. There is a parallel in inner-child therapy: knowing what the younger part needs is not enough when one is so absorbed in the child-state that adult perspective is insufficient to offer it.
cards.H-CHICKEN: The writer is encountering a chicken-and-egg dilemma. A person may be so far inside their child-state they cannot become the needed adult. Providing love is easier if one can already access at least one of their adult roles. Without that, the person might try speaking loving words while the inherited critic, numbness, panic, or urge to escape dominates the process.

sources.H-SOM: Physical trauma reactions can persist after the danger has passed, even when you know you're safe. With complex or developmental trauma, direct work on the deepest memory can be overwhelming, so a gradual approach may be enough: Buddhist nun Pema Chodron calls it a “feather touch,” and Peter Levine, the founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle work around the edges “pendulation.” The same limit appears in inner-child therapy: you can know what the younger part needs yet enter the child-state so fully that too little adult perspective remains to provide it.
sources.H-CHICKEN: But here’s the chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so far inside the child-state that you can’t become the adult? This is much easier when you can already reach one of those adult roles. Without that, you can sit there trying to say all the loving things while the old critic, numbness, panic, or urge to get away is running the whole thing.
